You explain cause and consequence (perché, siccome, dato che, grazie a, a causa di, quindi, perciò, così… che) to say why something happened and what followed.
since, as (at the start of the sentence)
Since it's raining, I'm staying at home.

The train is late because of the snow.

To express cause with perché, siccome, poiché, dato che, visto che.
To put "siccome" at the start of the sentence: Siccome piove, resto a casa.
To use grazie a, a causa di, per colpa di + noun.
To express consequence with quindi, perciò, allora, così.
To use così… che / tanto… che (so… that).
To ask about a cause with "perché?" and "come mai?".
Florence, 5th October. Matei and Giulia came back from their honeymoon a week ago. Professor Bellini calls them into his office.
Sit down. I called you in because I have important news.
On the contrary. Seeing that you didn't manage to rest on your honeymoon, you sent me a ten-page report on the Caravaggio in Syracuse.
They were just a few observations. The painting needs restoring, so…
So I sent it to the Heritage Authority in Syracuse. And thanks to your report, they've found the funding. They want you to do the restoration.
Us? But why us, of all people?
Because you know that painting better than anyone. And because I'm too old to work in such a cold church.
In February. It will take six months, so you'll be back in Florence in August.
Six months… from February… Professor, may I think about it for a few days?
Think about it? Esposito, it's a Caravaggio! But all right. Since it's the first time you've ever asked me for time, I'll give you a week.
Giulia, are you all right? You're so pale you look like a fresco.
I'm just tired. It must be the journey.
Stress on the last syllable, with a closed "e": per-KAY, poy-KAY. CH = "k".
GU + E = "gweh" run together: kon-se-GWEN-tsa. ZZ = a long "ts".
Double FF and LL, held slightly longer: af-FRES-ko, PAL-lee-da.
1. Cause: perché, siccome, poiché, dato che
at the START of the sentence
Poiché piove, la partita è rinviata.
"Siccome" almost always goes at the start: "Siccome sono stanca, vado a letto." NOT "Vado a letto siccome sono stanca" — there you say "perché".
"Perché" means both "why?" and "because", as in the question and the answer: "Perché ridi?" — "Perché sono felice."
2. Grazie a, a causa di, per colpa di + noun
With a noun (not a verb), cause is expressed with set phrases. The preposition merges with the article:
Grazie alla vostra relazione, abbiamo i soldi.
Il treno è in ritardo a causa della neve.
because of, through the fault of (someone is to blame)
Abbiamo perso l’aereo per colpa di Matei.
Don't forget to merge: grazie AL professore, a causa DELLA pioggia, per colpa DEI ritardi. NOT "a causa di la pioggia".
Sono stanca, quindi vado a letto.
Durerà sei mesi, perciò tornerete in agosto.
Pioveva, così siamo rimasti a casa.
I costi sono aumentati; di conseguenza, il prezzo sale.
"Allora" very often opens a line in speech: "Allora, cominciamo?" = "So, shall we start?".
To say something is so intense that it has a consequence, put "così / tanto / talmente" before the adjective and "che" before the consequence:
She was so tired that she fell asleep on the train.
I ate so much that I can't move.
The painting is so beautiful that it looks alive.
"That" (of consequence) is "che", NOT "come" or "quanto": "così pallida CHE sembri un affresco".
"Come mai?" = "how come?", a question about cause that is more casual and more surprised than "perché?". There's no inversion after "come mai":
I'm staying at home because I'm tired.
We have the money thanks to your report.
I've finished work, so I can go out.
She was so tired that she fell asleep.
We missed the plane because of Matei.
Siccome sono stanca, vado a letto.
Vado a letto siccome sono stanca.
Siccome vado a letto sono stanca.
The cause is someone's fault: "We're late because of the traffic."
Siamo in ritardo per colpa del traffico.
Siamo in ritardo grazie al traffico.
Siamo in ritardo perciò il traffico.
It will take six months, so you'll be back in August.
Perché Bellini ha chiamato Matei e Giulia?
Che cosa gli hanno mandato dalla Sicilia?
Grazie a che cosa la Soprintendenza ha trovato i soldi?

La chiesa è troppo fredda per lui

They had been back from Sicily for two weeks, and Giulia was always tired. In the mornings she couldn't get up. Since she was usually the one who woke Matei, he had realised at once that something was wrong. "It's because of the trip," Giulia said. "Ten days of sun are more tiring than a month of work."

Then came the nausea. On the first day Giulia blamed Graziella's coffee, which in her opinion had become too strong. On the second day she blamed the cannoli they had brought back from Syracuse. On the third day she blamed the Florentine rain. Matei always believed her, because Giulia always had an explanation for everything.

At the workshop it was worse. The smell of the solvents, which she had never even noticed before, was now so strong that she had to work with the window open. Bellini watched her without saying anything. One day Giulia arrived twenty minutes late. The professor looked at his watch, then at her. "Esposito," was all he said, "since you haven't been late once in three years, I won't say anything today."

Pietro had noticed something too. "How come Giulia doesn't eat ribollita any more?" he asked his grandmother one evening. "She used to eat two plates of it. Now she says it smells strange. But ribollita doesn't smell strange. Ribollita is perfect." Graziella didn't answer. She just smiled, and put a little ginger in the tea.

The next day, while Matei was at the library, Graziella called Giulia into the kitchen. She gave her a cup of ginger tea and a little plate of crackers. "Sip it slowly," she told her. "Ginger tea saved my life when I was expecting Marco." Giulia looked at her with wide eyes. "Graziella… why are you telling me this?" "Because I have eyes, sweetheart. And because at my age you understand some things before the people living them do."

That afternoon Giulia didn't go to the pharmacy on via Maggio, because the pharmacist there knew everyone and talked to everyone. She went to a pharmacy on the other side of the Arno, near Santa Croce, where nobody knew her. She bought a test, a bottle of water and, so as not to look suspicious, a toothpaste she didn't need.

At home, alone, she waited three minutes that felt like three hours. Then she looked. Two lines. She sat down on the edge of the bath and looked again, because she wasn't sure she had seen properly. There were still two. So she went out onto the terrace, where Totò, her plant, was, and sat down next to him.

"So that's why," she said to Totò. "It wasn't the coffee. It wasn't the cannoli. And the Florentine rain isn't to blame at all." Totò, as usual, didn't answer. Giulia laughed, then cried a little, then laughed again. She was so happy and so scared that she didn't know what to do with her hands.

Then she did the maths. If the baby was born in May, she couldn't work in Syracuse from February to August, in a cold church, on scaffolding six metres high, surrounded by solvents. So she would have to say no to Bellini. No to Caravaggio. She felt a little pang in her heart. But then she put a hand on her stomach, and the pang went away.

Now the problem was a different one: how to tell Matei? She wanted to do it in a special way, because he had asked her to marry him on a bridge, in the snow. She couldn't tell him in the bathroom, holding a useless toothpaste.

At that moment she heard Matei's footsteps on the stairs. He was whistling, as he always did when he was happy. Giulia put the test in her pocket and went back inside. Matei was holding an enormous book. "Look what I found at the library! Everything about Caravaggio in Sicily. Thanks to this book, by February we'll already know everything!"

Giulia kissed him. "Sunday," she said. "On Sunday, at lunch at Graziella's, I'll tell you something." "What?" "Something more important than Caravaggio." Matei laughed. "There's nothing more important than Caravaggio." Giulia smiled and touched her pocket. "We'll see," she said.
"aspettavo Marco" = I was expecting Marco (I was pregnant)
"non le serviva" = she didn't need it
"fare i conti" = to do the maths
